newsitem.title: USA: CPUC investigating PG&E tree trimming funds.
newsitem.headline: CPUC investigating PG&E tree trimming funds.

text.p: The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) is investigating charges that PG&E Corp's Pacific Gas & Electric Co diverted $80 million in tree-trimming funds to executive bonuses, the state agency's consumer services enforcement division said Thursday.

The charges stem from a Nevada County criminal trial which ended in June when PG&E was found guilty of causing a 1994 forest fire by neglecting to trim trees, one of which touched a high-voltage power line and ignited a blaze near the town of Rough and Ready, Calif.

The prosecutor in that trial said PG&E gave the money to managers to reward cost cutting, but the CPUC waited until a verdict was reached to launch its investigation, Larry McNeely, chief of the CPUC division, said.
"PG&E's tree-trimming has not kept up with vegetation growth. There have been incidents in which fires have been caused," he noted.
McNeely added the agency was "disappointed by what we saw in the criminal trial. We were distressed that 11 citizens lost their homes."
But PG&E said it has nothing to hide.
"If the CPUC wants to investigate, of course we will participate and answer any questions they have," PG&E spokesman Leonard Anderson said.
Any adjustments to PG&E's cost allocations could be part of the utility's next general rate case, which will be filed later this year, he noted.
Anderson explained the utility will from time to time shift money from one business purpose to another but tree-trimming funds "did not go directly into bonuses or anything like that."
Between 1987 and 1996, PG&E spent roughly $550 million on vegetation management, exceeding the approximate $517 million authorized by the CPUC, the spokesman said.
This year PG&E will spend about $126 million, he added.
McNeely said he hopes to have a report on the investigation ready for the CPUC by the end of September.
Separately, PG&E has agreed to reimburse the community of Los Gatos, Calif., more than $2 million for damage from a fire last week in the Santa Clara County community.

Ignition of the more recent fire was not, however, caused by wayward tree limbs but by a surge in an overhead power line which followed a truck's collision with a power pole more than a mile from where the fire began, PG&E's Anderson explained.
"We will reimburse uninsured fire victimes for reasonable value and cover the cost of fire suppression," he said.
"Then we plan to go after the third party who hit the pole."
